title: Water pressure, roof materials and damage prevention
audience: Trainee or new worker on the roof soft washing track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to water pressure, roof materials and damage prevention.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instruction.heading: Pressure is a damage question as well as a cleaning question
instruction.body: Water pressure can do more harm than it removes. The same jet that lifts growth from a roof can crack a tile, strip a coating from metal, drive water under the overlap of a sheet, tear a sealant bead, or erode the mortar that holds a ridge in place. Once the damage is done, water can reach the roof space and the rooms below, often out of sight. Pressure equipment also carries its own hazards. WorkSafe Victoria's safety alert on high-pressure water jetting describes injuries from a jet piercing the skin, from flying debris, from a hose whipping or a coupling separating, and from falls. For a soft-washing worker the first lesson is that the method is chosen to protect the roof and the people around it. A higher pressure is never a shortcut to a better result.

instruction.heading: Roof materials and what each one tolerates
instruction.body: Each material has its own weak points. Concrete and clay tiles depend on their bedding, their mortar and their interlock, and a jet directed under the lap of a tile can lift it. Metal sheeting depends on its coating, its fixings and its overlaps. A high-pressure stream can remove the coating and expose bare metal, and water forced under sheets can reach the framing and the ceiling below. Fibre-cement sheeting can be brittle, and an older product may contain asbestos, so it must not be abraded or blasted. Refer a suspected sheet for assessment as described in the earlier lessons. Slate and some natural stones are prone to cracking under impact. Polycarbonate and acrylic rooflights can scratch, craze or yellow, and they count as openings under the rules in the previous lesson. Membranes and bituminous surfaces are sensitive to abrasion, and the loss of surface granules or the peeling of sealant are signs of damage. Where the material has not been identified, the method cannot be chosen, and the work is held.

instruction.heading: Choosing a limit and a method
instruction.body: No pressure setting appears in this lesson, and none should be chosen from the worker's own judgement. The limit comes from three places: the roof material manufacturer's guidance, the rating of the equipment and its fittings, and the authorised method for the job. Where any of those is missing, the answer is not to test a higher setting until something works. The answer is to hold the work and find the limit. Low-pressure soft washing works mainly through contact time and gentle application, not through force. A worker who feels the need for more force should stop and ask whether the product, the method or the surface is the real problem. A method that cannot be explained in terms of the material and its limit is not an authorised method.

instruction.heading: Damage prevention in practice
instruction.body: Damage prevention is mostly about direction and the path of the water. Keep the spray at a low angle so the stream does not run under laps, seams or the edge of a flashing. Do not aim the jet at sealant, at the edges of tiles, or at gaps where water could enter a cavity. Move steadily and do not dwell on one spot. Keep debris moving away from gutters, downpipes and vents, rather than pushing it into a blocked outlet that will overflow onto the wall or the ground. Stop water entering a roof cavity, a vent or a meter box, and check the area below the work for any sign of water. Before the job starts, photograph the roof and record existing damage, such as loose tiles, cracked sheets and failed sealant. A record made before work is what allows a later question about damage to be answered from evidence rather than memory.

instruction.heading: Equipment checks and pressure safety
instruction.body: Equipment must be checked before each use. Inspect hoses for cuts, bulges and worn covers. Check couplings, fittings and the nozzle. Confirm that every component is rated at or above the equipment's maximum pressure and is compatible with the rest of the set, and record the check. WorkSafe Victoria's alert says operators should wear at least safety glasses and a face shield, that people nearby need eye protection, and that the operator needs body armour where injury is possible. It also says that equipment and its attachments must not be modified without written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person, and that repairs are for the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person. The alert sets training and refresher expectations and names the standard AS/NZS 4233.1 for systems. This lesson does not authorise anyone to operate pressure equipment.

instruction.heading: Signs to stop and what to record
instruction.body: Stop work in the affected area, and record it, when you see a tile lifting or cracking, a coating coming away from a sheet, sealant peeling or pulling, water being driven under laps or into a joint, mortar crumbling, granules lost from a bituminous surface, a rooflight crazing or cracking, or water appearing inside the building. Do not keep working to see whether the damage gets worse. Mark the area, tell the supervisor, and let the decision owner set the next step. The record should show the photograph, the location, the time, and whether the damage was there before work began or appeared during it. A worker records what is visible. The cause and the repair are for the people competent to decide them.

instruction.heading: Run-off and where the water goes
instruction.body: Pressure and chemical washing both send water somewhere. Before work starts, identify where the run-off will go: gardens, lawns, stormwater pits, pools, water tanks, neighbouring properties and footpaths. Water that carries product or fine debris is an environmental concern as well as a damage concern. The operational rule for now is to hold the work wherever run-off cannot be controlled, and to record the path on the job plan.

procedure: Identify the roof material on each plane from the job pack and the photographs, and record the basis of each identification.
For each material, confirm the pressure or method limit from the manufacturer's guidance or the authorised method. If no limit is confirmed, hold the pressure element.
Check the equipment record for hoses, couplings, fittings and nozzle, confirm each rating, and remove any unrated or faulty item from use.
Photograph and record existing damage on each plane before any work is planned, and place it in the damage register.
Plan the water path so that the spray stays at a low angle and clear of laps, seams, flashings, sealant and cracked or loose areas.
Keep debris and water away from gutters, downpipes, roof cavities, vents and meter boxes, and record the run-off path on the job plan.
Stop the affected area if any sign of damage appears, and tell the supervisor before resuming.
Photograph the same locations after the work and record any new damage, with the people told.

workedExamples.situation: A concrete tile roof has cracked tiles and loose mortar at the ridge. The owner asks for high pressure to clear green growth quickly.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the response to the owner, and what happens to the cracked and loose areas?
workedExamples.reasoning: Decline the high-pressure request. Tile bedding and cracked units cannot be shown to take it, and no authorised limit is confirmed for this material. Explain that the method will use the approved product and gentle application. Hold the cracked and loose areas, photograph them before work, and mark them on the plan. Record the owner's request, the response and who was told. Do not test a higher setting on a spare tile to see what happens.

workedExamples.situation: A painted corrugated metal roof shows rust spots and a few loose screws. The plan calls for a pressure jetter across the whole roof.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the jetter be used, and what is the alternative?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the jetter on the coated sheet. High pressure can strip the coating and expose metal that will rust, and water can be driven under the overlaps to the framing and the ceiling below. The loose screws are a fixing question for a competent person. Record the rust spots and the loose screws with photographs, check whether the equipment and the product method are authorised for this coating, and hold the pressure element until the material limit is confirmed. Use a low-pressure method only if the authorised method covers this material.

workedExamples.situation: Before a wash, a worker finds a polycarbonate rooflight with fine crazing and a sheet scratched by an earlier brush. The plan says to brush the rooflight clean.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the worker do with the rooflight?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not brush the rooflight or wash it with pressure. The crazing and scratches show the sheet is already damaged and may be weaker than it looks. The rooflight is an opening and an exclusion zone under the earlier lesson. Photograph it, record it as existing damage, and keep the water path clear of it. Tell the supervisor so that a competent person can decide whether it needs repair before any work near it.

equipmentAndPpe: Safety glasses or goggles for the operator, with a face shield where the risk assessment or the product requires it.
Eye protection for anyone nearby, and body armour for the operator where there is a risk of injury, as WorkSafe Victoria's alert describes.
Gloves, protective clothing and any respirator that the product's SDS and the risk assessment require. See the chemical lesson.
Hearing protection where noise calls for it, and safe enclosed footwear.
A pre-use equipment checklist for hoses, couplings, fittings and nozzle, completed before each use.
A tag or label for any item removed from use, so that it cannot be used by mistake.
A pre-work photograph set and a damage register for each roof plane.

commonErrors.error: Using high pressure on tiles, metal or coated surfaces.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the material limit and the authorised method first. Where no limit is confirmed, hold the pressure element.

commonErrors.error: Aiming the jet at laps, seams, flashings or sealant.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the spray at a low angle and clear of overlaps, seams, flashings and sealant.

commonErrors.error: Pushing debris into gutters or blocked outlets.
commonErrors.prevention: Move debris away from downpipes and outlets, and record the run-off path before work.

commonErrors.error: Fitting an unrated fitting or changing the nozzle or attachment without approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only rated, compatible parts. Do not modify equipment or attachments without written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person.

commonErrors.error: Starting work without recording the existing damage.
commonErrors.prevention: Photograph and log all existing damage before any water is applied.

commonErrors.error: Continuing after a sign of damage to see whether it is serious.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the affected area, record it, and tell the supervisor before resuming.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and authority notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to operate high-pressure equipment, to work on a roof, or to carry out chemical application. Check your state or territory regulator, and obtain your employer's written authorisation before work starts.

High-pressure jetting hazards: WorkSafe Victoria's alert on high-pressure water jetting (published 14 September 2022, reviewed 11 May 2023) names jet injection, debris, hose whip, separated couplings, falls, chemical exposure, noise and electric shock as hazards. It asks employers to assess each job and provide suitable protective equipment, and it asks that every part be rated at or above the equipment's maximum pressure.

Modification and repair: Equipment and its attachments must not be modified without written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person. Only the manufacturer, its agent or a competent person should repair or maintain pressure equipment, according to WorkSafe Victoria's alert.

Fibre-cement and asbestos: WorkSafe Tasmania's licensing page says a licence is needed to remove any amount of friable asbestos, and to remove more than 10 square metres of non-friable asbestos (last updated 11 November 2025). Whether the licence rules name roof sheeting as a separate category is not confirmed by an official source. The WorkSafe ACT asbestos licensing page does not mention a size threshold, so whether the 10 square metre limit applies in the ACT is not confirmed by an official source. WorkSafe Victoria's asbestos page (reviewed 9 May 2024; no last-updated date shown) allows unlicensed removal of non-friable material only if the quantity does not exceed 10 square metres and the work takes no more than 1 hour in any 7-day period. As a working rule in this course, suspected fibre-cement is not abraded, blasted or pressure-cleaned until a competent assessment has been carried out. This lesson does not grant an asbestos licence or clearance.
Run-off and discharge: Pressure and chemical washing send water to the ground, drains and neighbouring land. Hold any work where run-off cannot be controlled.
Roof access and height: The roof access and height rules in the earlier lessons still apply. This lesson does not authorise any work on a roof, from a ladder, or from an elevated work platform.

Stop-work rule: Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if a tile, sheet, coating, sealant or rooflight shows damage, if water is driven under laps or into a cavity, if an item of equipment is damaged or unrated, or if the work falls outside your authorisation.

qualityStandard: The roof material is identified for each plane, and a pressure or method limit is recorded for each material. Where no limit is confirmed, the pressure element is held.
The equipment check record lists every hose, coupling, fitting and nozzle with its rating, and shows any item removed from use.
No jet is directed under laps, seams or flashings, at sealant, or into cracked or loose areas.
Pre-work and post-work photographs show the same locations, and any new damage is recorded and reported.
No equipment is modified and no unrated fitting is used.
Each run-off path is recorded, and any path that cannot be controlled holds the work.
documentationEvidence: A roof material register by plane, with the basis of each identification and the source of each method limit.
An equipment pre-use check record with the rating of each part and a record of any item removed from use.
Pre-work and post-work photographs with the date, location and plane label, with the original files kept.
A damage register listing existing and new damage, its location, and who was told.
Run-off path notes recorded on the job plan.
summary: Pressure is a damage risk to the roof and to the water path. The method does the cleaning, not force.
The limit comes from the material, the equipment rating and the authorised method. Where none is confirmed, the work is held.
Photograph and record the roof before work, and stop at any sign of damage, lifting, cracking or water driven under laps.
Check equipment before use, never modify it without written approval, and leave its operation to someone authorised to do it.

knowledgeChecks.question: A concrete tile roof has cracked tiles and loose mortar at the ridge. The owner asks for high pressure to finish quickly. What is correct?
options: Use the highest setting the equipment allows, to lift the growth faster on the whole roof surface.
Decline high pressure, check the material and method limits, and hold any cracked or loose area.
Use high pressure only on tiles away from the ridge line and the edges, where the roof is in good order
Ask the owner to sign a release and proceed on the highest setting for the whole roof today

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about hoses and fittings on high-pressure equipment is correct?
options: A fitting that screws onto the hose thread is suitable for the job at hand, whatever the rating
A fitting must be rated at or above the equipment's maximum pressure and be compatible with the rest of the set.
A cheaper fitting can be used if it looks the same as the original one on the machine and fits the thread
A visual check once a year is enough to confirm the hose and all the fittings are safe for use on the job

knowledgeChecks.question: An operator wants to fit a nozzle attachment that the manufacturer does not list. What should happen?
options: Fit it, since similar attachments have worked before on other roofs and other jobs in the past without any issue
Fit it and tell the client afterwards, once the wash has been finished, checked and signed off as complete
Do not modify the equipment or its attachments without written approval from the manufacturer or a competent person.
Fit it for the first job only, then remove it before the second job starts on the same roof again

knowledgeChecks.question: During a test on a metal roof, water is driven under the laps. What is the correct action?
options: Continue at a lower angle, because the water will drain away from the laps and seams once it moves
Stop, redirect the water away from laps and seams, and record the observation before any further work.
Increase the pressure to clear the laps and push the water through them quickly and fully
Ignore it if the sheets look intact from the ground, since they seem fine to the eye for now
